One edge of the instrument is uneven and saw-toothed, and is scraped to produce a sharp sound. It is played with two beaters, one of wood or bamboo used only for scraping the toothed edge and the other for striking the body. The bamboo chamber gives a natural resonance, so the instrument carries well in the open.
Tagutok的音色具有明亮而尖銳的特徵，帶有明顯的節奏感。其音質粗礪而乾燥，富: The tagutok sounds bright and sharp, with a strong sense of rhythm. The tone is rough and dry and carries well, so it travels clearly across open rice fields. Scraping the toothed edge produces a sharp scraping sound, while striking gives a heavier knock, and the two sounds complement each other. Its range lies in the middle and upper frequencies, and it has plenty of attack. The resonance depends on the natural resonance of the bamboo chamber; beside a metal gong the timbre is gentler and rougher, but it has richer overtones than plain wooden percussion. This mixture of sounds lets it both drive birds away effectively and give a steady rhythmic base for social dancing.

The Tagutok (provisional name) is a Philippine bamboo scraped gong / slit drum, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.2, an idiophone. It is built with a saw-toothed edge on one side and is played with two beaters: one scrapes the toothed edge, the other strikes the beat. The Maguindanaon and the Visayans use instruments of this kind; the Maguindanaon and the Banuwaen use it in the rice fields to scare birds away with its sound. The Maguindanaon and the Bukidnon peoples have also used it on social occasions to play simple dance rhythms, usually a single rhythm pattern and sometimes combined with another. The rice-field use is no longer practised.
卡古爾（Tagutok）是菲律賓南部民族的古老竹製樂器，起源於棉蘭老島地區。馬京: The Tagutok is an old bamboo instrument of the peoples of the southern Philippines, originating in the Mindanao region. The Maguindanaon and the Visayans were the first to use it, and its distinctive design reflects the ingenuity of the indigenous peoples of the area. In an agricultural society it played an important role: the Maguindanaon and the Banuwaen used its sharp, piercing sound to drive birds from the rice fields and protect the harvest. Over time its uses widened to social occasions, and the Maguindanaon and the Bukidnon began to use it to accompany traditional dances, the rhythm of striking and scraping giving musical support to simple dances. The Tagutok has thus become an important marker of the culture of the southern Philippines, reflecting the region's path from a practical farming tool to a form of cultural and artistic expression.
